newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Sinn Fein's Adams counters Irish PM's attack.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein's Adams counters Irish PM's attack.

text.p: Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams, smarting from an attack by Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, said on Thursday he was not a member of the Irish Republican Army (IRA).
"I am not a member of the IRA," Adams told the Irish Republic's RTE broadcasting network. Asked if he had ever been, the Northern Ireland nationalist leader replied: "No."
He was reacting to a statement by Bruton on Wednesday night that a vote for Sinn Fein in British elections on May 1 would be a vote for IRA violence aimed at ending British rule of Northern Ireland.

Bruton's statement brought relations between the Irish government and Sinn Fein, the IRA's political backers, to a new low because of the guerrillas' decision to end a 17-month ceasefire in February last year.
Bruton counselled Northern Ireland voters not to support Sinn Fein candidates at the British election because, he said, the party and the IRA were inextricably linked.

"It would be hypocrisy to pretend that a vote for Sinn Fein is anything other than a vote for the IRA," Bruton said after talks with John Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour (SDLP) party of Northern Ireland.

The SDLP shares the IRA and Sinn Fein goal of uniting Ireland under Dublin's rule but its central policy platform is non-violence and a commitment to agreement between minority Catholics and pro-British Protestants in Northern Ireland.
Adams accused Bruton of "blatant electioneering" in Irish elections which must be held by November and in which the crumbling Northern Ireland peace process is expected to be an issue.

Sinn Fein is contesting several Northern Ireland seats in the British poll and expects to win up to three. But it will not occupy seats in the London parliament because that would entail allegiance to Britain, which it sees as an illegal colonial ruler.
It says voters should return Sinn Fein candidates to show the British government that the party's call to be admitted to round-table peace talks without any preconditions has significant backing.

But Bruton's comments were directed at Sinn Fein's long-standing claim that it is a separate organisation from the IRA. Sinn Fein says it abhors violence but understands those who resort to it to end British rule.
Adams complained that Bruton had singled out IRA violence, which included a suspected attack on British army posts in Northern Ireland a few hours earlier. No-one was hurt.
"How can he (Bruton) talk to the British government which is heavily involved in violence in our society?" he asked.
"I live in Belfast. I am phoning you from Belfast. I am surrounded by British forces of occupation. I want to see the British out of my country. They have no right to be here," Adams said.

Adams declined to be drawn on media speculation that the IRA would call a truce close to the May 1 British election in an attempt to get the next British government to end a ban on its participation in peace talks, which resume on June 3.
It is banned from the negotiations between the SDLP and pro-British Unionists because of IRA violence.
